brief.head: Moth in disguise
brief.text: A moth in a poisonous insect’s colours is isomorphic mimicry, Ajay Shah said: an agency full of pomp, empty inside. In the other failure, the inside is staffed but malfunctions. {082-C02}

brief.head: Born with a watchdog
brief.text: Every American federal agency has an inspector general who can investigate its highest bosses, Ajay Shah said. Built over a hundred years, it is simply taken for granted. {082-C04}

brief.head: STEM is the easy bit
brief.text: Technical knowledge has a finite set of books and can be examined, Ajay Shah said. “What exam is going to test that you understand epistemology?” {082-C08}

brief.head: Plan for the worst
brief.text: The state should be designed so the worst ruler can do little damage, Amit Varma said. Ajay Shah said every healthcare expert must trace the failures back to the constitution. {082-C13}

brief.head: More calls that work
brief.text: Economic development, Ajay Shah said, is an ever-expanding range of public-goods capabilities, private contracting and contract enforcement, so that more complex firms can take root in India. {082-C15}

thought.text: You will know everything about nothing.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, warning against the modern temptation to over-specialise

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on why good policies fail to travel
lead.head: Lost in transplantation
body: A policy that works in Norway or France will not necessarily work in India. The reason, Ajay Shah argued, is invisible infrastructure: the hundred other systems on which any policy quietly depends.

Amit Varma, who has been urging his co-host to write a book on the idea, opened by welcoming listeners to *The Seen and the Unseen*. No, he added, this was not a crossover: the episode was simply about unseen things.

Shah began with a military affairs geek who falls for the Norwegian military and wants to bring its manuals and procedures to India, or an admirer of TSMC who would replicate it in Bombay. “And the thing is this stuff doesn’t work,” he said.
## Blind spots

The supporting systems are not hidden, Shah said. Courts, the rule of law, product liability, government HR and contracting are all there to be seen. They are invisible because specialists do not look at them. {082-C01}
“If you only bother to look, all the things are there,” he said. “But the thing is that the people who are specialists tend to be blind about them.”

He offered a software analogy. Every institution makes API calls to capabilities it does not own: a military calls on pensions, a hospital on product liability and the courts. In rich countries the calls return. Under underdevelopment, they fail or work only sometimes. {082-C03}

Court calls make the point. A medical malpractice case in the UK, Shah guessed, has about an 80 per cent chance of being decided correctly. In India it is “almost a coin toss”, and the mess reshapes the whole healthcare system.

Privacy shows the cost of ignoring all this. Advanced economies spent the 20th century building checks on the state, so Western blogs worry about Google’s targeted ads, which Shah considers a trivial problem. Indians who learnt privacy from those blogs carried the debate in the wrong direction. {082-C06}
“In the Indian context, there is only one problem to solve,” he said. “How to shut down state access to information about the people.”

Seasoned practitioners are no cure. Someone with twenty years at the Bank of England, Shah said, borrowing from Lant Pritchett, knows as much about policy design as a New York taxi driver knows about how cars work.
## What is to be done
Shah’s remedies began with a warning: be wary of specialisation. Narrow depth is the easy path and makes you less useful. Breadth is harder.
Next, he recommended “an obscure YouTube show by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah”.

Then take public choice theory seriously. Don’t assume the French doctor or the Norwegian general is a good guy. Ask why the doctor won’t overprescribe for a kickback from the X-ray clinic, and the answers will lead to the invisible infrastructure.
Think locally: before transplanting French healthcare into Haryana, know whether a truck carrying expensive goods can travel a given road at night.
Sometimes, do nothing. State capability, Shah said, is a very finite muscle, and many times the wise answer is to shrink the scope of the Indian state. {082-C11}
And fix the foundations every sector stands on, government HR above all: fix it everywhere, Shah said, and hundreds of agencies will work better. {082-C14}
## The last word
The episode ended on a joke from Shah’s list. “And also the YouTube shows that expand the discourse,” Varma said. “How could you forget that?”
Shah agreed. “To get to those three things, you need great YouTube shows.”

second.label: The name of the show
second.head: Name that tune
second.deck: Two favourite songs offered titles; one phrase also described how the hosts think
body: When Amit Varma and Ajay Shah were choosing a name for their show, they took two candidates from favourite songs. One was John Lennon’s *Watching the Wheels*. {082-R10}
The other came from Bruce Springsteen’s *You’re Missing*. Varma picked its phrase, everything is everything, and Shah said that the song resonated with him too. {082-S07}

Varma told the story while riffing on C.L.R. James: “What do they know of cricket, who only cricket know.” James, he had recently found, was himself riffing on Rudyard Kipling. {082-J11} Swap cricket for any word, Varma said, and the line holds. That, he said, is really why the show is called *Everything is Everything*.

quote.text: When we put the songs aside, everything is everything just made sense because that’s how we try to think about the world.

second.caption: how the show got its name

third.head: Driving isn’t designing
body: Lant Pritchett, Ajay Shah said, has an analogy for the seasoned first-world practitioner. A New York taxi driver knows how to sit in a car, turn the steering wheel and press the brakes. {#taxi}

He doesn’t know why cars are built as they are, or what trade-offs shaped the brakes. A veteran of the Norwegian military likewise takes for granted five hundred years of liberal democracy, in which an Armed Forces Special Powers Act is unimaginable.
Or take twenty years at the New York Fed. “They know the how. But they don’t know the why,” he said. “And the why is an incentive story.” {082-S03}
Yet Indians, Shah said, lend such people institutional legitimacy because they have worked twenty years at the Bank of England. “The answer is no.”
third.caption: the New York taxi driver

p2.title: What lies beneath
p2.deck: Ajay Shah on the systems every policy rests on, and what India should do about them. {082-C01}

sections.label: The idea
sections.head: What the specialist can’t see
sections.caption: the invisible infrastructure
body: Good policies, Ajay Shah said, do not travel well. A military affairs geek who loves the Norwegian military may want to bring over its manuals and its tactics, techniques and procedures. An admirer of TSMC may want to replicate it in Bombay. Neither, he said, would work.
Amit Varma said Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok had made much the same point in a paper whose title he nearly got rudely wrong: *Premature Imitation and India’s Flailing State*. {082-J02}
Varma reached for a biological term, isomorphic mimicry. Shah drew a distinction.
## Hollow or broken

In mimicry, a harmless moth wears the colours of a poisonous insect so that birds leave it alone. India’s version, Shah said, is a fancy building called a theatre command, a central bank or a food safety regulator, with all the pomp, headcount and conference rooms of its first-world namesake, but none of the people, processes, checks and incentives.

Invisible-infrastructure failure is different. You honestly try to build a Bank of England in India, and it flounders anyway. “Here inside it’s not empty, but it’s actually malfunctioning,” Shah said. {082-C02}
~ Varma suggested the two sit on a continuum. He also had a Hindi summary of the hollow kind: a central bank on the outside, hollow on the inside.

quote.text: So here you have something that doesn’t work in practice, and so we should understand why it doesn’t work in theory.

sections.label: Three lenses
sections.head: When the call doesn’t return
sections.caption: institutions making API calls
body: Ajay Shah’s first lens came from software. Every institution makes demands on capabilities elsewhere in the economy, like an API call. When the French healthcare system buys something, it relies on product safety and liability rules made by others. {082-C03}
In rich countries the calls just work. Under underdevelopment, he said, the capabilities either don’t exist or you are “standing on shifting sands” and the call is unreliable.

Pensions are his example. India’s military reforms got tripped up because military pensions were not solved as part of wider pension reform. With a sound, economy-wide defined contribution system, Amit Varma said, the military would be like an application that plugs into it.
## Who watches the canteen

The second lens is incentives. Nobody is a saint, and the surroundings shape what people maximise. A canteen vendor in the Norwegian military, Shah said, is unlikely even to imagine corruption in food procurement. In India the conditions are different.
The third is checks and balances, many of them inherited. Every American federal agency gets an inspector general, a system built over a hundred years. {082-C04}
~ Courts are a call too. Shah guessed a UK malpractice case is decided correctly 80 per cent of the time. In India, he said, it is “almost a coin toss”. {#coin}

quote.text: So think of that as an API call that each piece of the policy ecosystem requires other pieces to work.

sections.label: What is to be done
sections.head: Five watts, one square micron
sections.caption: the trouble with specialisation
body: Ajay Shah named his plan after Lenin’s manifesto *What Is to Be Done*, having first quoted, tongue in cheek, “the great man Karl Marx”. With hindsight, Amit Varma replied, it was what is not to be done. {082-J10}

The first item: be wary of specialisation. Every incentive of the modern world, Shah said, pushes people to dive deep, because expertise earns respect. {082-C07} Narrow depth is the easy path and makes you less useful. Better to have breadth, and the horsepower to master anything in a couple of weeks when needed.

Shah and a colleague once agreed, with a look, that STEM is easy and humanities is hard. By humanities, Varma said, they meant learning the human condition through books, world cinema and music, not university departments.
## Technician or thinker
Narrow depth, Shah said, makes you a technician, a cog in the wheel. Leaders like it: they want people who shut up and execute. That suits the principal, not always the agent. {082-C09}
Varma was blunter. Over-specialised people, he said, will have work got out of them for a while. “After that, they’ll get it done from AI.” {082-J15}
~ He generalised C.L.R. James: what do they know of X who only X know? Even depth, he said, needs breadth.

quote.text: The very essence of growing is developing breadth, is developing strategic sense, is rising from being a technician to being a thinker.

sections.label: Think locally
sections.head: Know the road at night
sections.caption: thinking locally
body: Before you transplant the French healthcare system into Haryana, Ajay Shah said, you must be deeply grounded in Haryana. Can a truck carrying expensive materials travel at night on such and such road? Only someone who lives there knows. {082-C10}
He called it authenticity, “the beautiful humanities word”: being embedded in a culture and a place, with a common-sense intuition for how it works.

Amit Varma’s example was Sowmya Dhanaraj, whose episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* is in his top ten. Her parents worked in a factory, and her mother sold tea at a stall on the Coimbatore Highway for many years. {082-S04}
## Rooted, not imported

Her education was the same as everyone else’s, Varma said, but her thinking comes from the bottom up, from the way India really is. That bedrock, he said, will help her craft good policy whatever she does.
The warning cuts both ways. Shah cautioned Indians who want to export Indian successes to Morocco or Mozambique, where the invisible infrastructure is very different.
~ Earlier, Varma had sketched the opposite type: born privileged in a big city, educated abroad, back with jargon and frames that don’t apply.

quote.text: She doesn’t have that elite education. She doesn’t have foreign ideas implanted into her brain. She’s seen the world. She’s asked the right questions.

sections.label: Do less
sections.head: The courage to walk away
sections.caption: the virtue of doing nothing
body: Ajay Shah confessed to being “a soft pinko”. In Sweden, with government expenditure at some fifty-five per cent of GDP, it is hard not to be impressed. {#sweden}
But state capability, he said, is a very finite muscle. It should be lavished on a few problems, and India should walk away from those that are unreasonably difficult or impossible in its conditions.
His example was defined benefit pensions. The correct answer, Shah said, is “four hundred years more until India becomes an advanced economy”. {#fourhundred}
## Rich first
Amit Varma drew on Johan Norberg: Scandinavian countries grew rich through free markets and entrepreneurship, and built welfare states only afterwards, while keeping business easy. {082-R14}

Lant Pritchett’s paper, Varma said, shows a ninety-nine per cent correlation between human welfare indicators and per capita GDP. Get the growth first, he argued, and redistribute once the pie is big enough. {082-C12}
India, Varma said, does many things badly instead of a few things well. Every intervention also has an opportunity cost: spend money here, and the state can’t spend it somewhere else.
~ A market failure, Varma added, is necessary for the state to act but not sufficient. Famines, humanitarian crises and pollution qualify; small stuff does not.

quote.text: Many, many times the wise answer is to shrink the scope of the Indian state.

sections.label: Fix the foundations
sections.head: Rocket first, payload later
sections.caption: the rocket and the payload
body: Ajay Shah’s last item was to work on foundations: the legal system, the rule of law, government HR and contracting, and checks on the state’s coercive power. “Coercive power is a poison,” he said.

In the book he wrote with Vijay Kelkar, *In Service of the Republic*, there is a rocket and payload analogy. Take the central statistical organisation. The payload is GDP measurement and questions like double deflation. The bulk of the organisation, its budgeting, public financial management, contracting and HR, is the rocket.
If the rocket fails, he said, there is no point being a subject matter expert on double deflation.
## Everyone’s problem

So fewer people should work on one domain and more on what cuts across all of them. A narrow specialist wants to run AIIMS properly. Someone who wants a more consequential life goes after government HR, because it is everywhere. {082-C14}
All these, he said, are high impact, because they help all the sectors.
~ Amit Varma tested the idea with a clumsy analogy of his own: toilets built under Swachh Bharat with no drainage. {082-S05}

quote.text: If we fix government HR all across the landscape, we will get hundreds of better functioning government agencies.

side.boxText: Amit Varma pointed to *Premature Imitation and India’s Flailing State* by Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok, which makes much the same argument. The term flailing state, he said, is taken from Lant Pritchett’s great work. {082-R01}

contQuote.text: Don’t say nobility, patriotism, those are all bad reasons. Think deeply about incentives. Why do people behave the way they behave, and that will take you to the invisible infrastructure.

p3.title: Tales of the unseen
p3.deck: Four stories of systems nobody noticed until they went missing

stories.start: The example I want to give you is the French healthcare system.
stories.end: And then sure enough, when you try Transplanting these things, they work pretty badly
stories.caption: the French healthcare system
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the system where the light bulb went off
stories.head: No French cure for India
body: Ajay Shah says the idea of invisible infrastructure clicked for him while studying one system: French healthcare. “For me personally, that was where some light bulb went off,” he said.

Rich countries have many problems in their healthcare systems, most notably the United States, which he said probably spends three times as much as other OECD countries and gets much worse outcomes. {#threex}

France is different. Its arrangement of public and private works rather well. Anyone with an interest in health, Shah said, will inevitably dig deeper, and then wonder whether India could have the same.

That is where the mistake lies. “The mistake around invisible infrastructure would be to start thinking that because XYZ design of the French healthcare system works so well in France, we could or should transplant that into India,” he said. {082-S01}

French healthcare, Shah argued, sits on a base of a hundred other subsystems: budgeting, the rule of law and its enforcement, product liability and liability in healthcare, the government’s HR and contracting, the behaviour of public and private. Each exerts tugs and pulls on the system.
None of this is hidden, he said: anyone who bothers to look can see the French courts and the government’s contracting. But specialists tend to be blind to them. {082-C01}
~ So healthcare people talk to healthcare people. The NHS is good at one thing, the French at another; each should steal the other’s ideas. Then, sure enough, the transplants work pretty badly.
stories.why: A successful institution is the visible top of a large stack of supporting systems. The specialist’s depth keeps that stack out of view, which is why the expert is often the one proposing a transplant that fails.
stories.postscript: For all his study, Shah admitted, he has not yet had a chance to visit France.

stories.start: This is called the fruit of the poisonous tree doctrine.
stories.end: is already very high even before the case reaches the courts
stories.caption: the fruit of the poisonous tree
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on an American rule that keeps police in check
stories.head: Tap illegally, lose the case
body: Suppose a law says a policeman needs a judge’s warrant before tapping your phone, Ajay Shah said. She taps it anyway, and finds proof that you are the murderer.
In the United States, he believes, judges settled this in 1938 with a bright-line test, the fruit of the poisonous tree doctrine: evidence obtained through illegal means is inadmissible. {#y1938}

Without it, he argued, police would never bother with warrants. If they found nothing, they would at least have blackmail material; if they found something, the ends would justify the means. {082-S02}

~ Amit Varma added a second safeguard: investigators and prosecutors sit in separate departments, and prosecutors judged on successful prosecutions won’t take weak cases. Shah noted that India has neither.

quote.text: If illegally obtained evidence is permissible in court, why would a cop ever take the permission?

stories.postscript: Anyone who has watched *Chicago PD* or *Law and Order*, Amit Varma said, knows evidence from an illegal search is not admissible. {082-J06}

stories.start: I did an episode on Swaj Bharat a long time ago with uh Shruti
stories.end: And to me, what uh we normalize them and they become invisible
stories.caption: the Swachh Bharat toilets
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a sanitation drive that forgot the drains
stories.head: A toilet with nowhere to go
body: Amit Varma recalled a point Shruti Rajagopalan made on his show *The Seen and the Unseen*. Under Swachh Bharat, toilets went up in villages all over the place, but often with no drainage system.
People in higher-caste houses would not touch their own refuse, so they got people from lower castes to do the job. The scheme, Varma said, exacerbated the caste system. {082-S05}

Ajay Shah was indignant. “What kind of water and sanitation person are you if you think that there’ll be toilet but you haven’t thought through how the water will come and how the sewage will go out?” {082-J18}
~ “This was not my decision,” Varma said. Drainage was visible, Shah objected. Things like drainage, water and electricity, Varma replied, become invisible because we normalise them.
stories.why: Every intervention, even a toilet, depends on systems around it: water coming in, sewage going out. Leave them out, and the fix can make the original problem worse, as the toilets did for caste.

stories.start: I remember when uh the Latour earthquakes happened, Japan sent some four hundred
stories.end: you can just normalize and assume it is there and things can go wrong
stories.caption: the air conditioners for Latur
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on aid that assumed the power was on
stories.head: Cool comfort for Latur
body: After the Latur earthquake, Amit Varma remembers, Japan sent some four hundred air conditioners as relief. {082-S06}
Most of those places didn’t even have electricity, he said, and even if they had, the survivors would not have needed air conditioners. It was “completely out of whack”.

Varma offered it as part of what he called a clumsy analogy. Any business, whether a factory, a services firm or a restaurant, makes API calls to water supply and electricity. {#apicalls} We normalise such things until they turn invisible.
~ And seen from the sky-high distance of an elite Ivy League education, he said, “you can just normalize and assume it is there and things can go wrong.”

quote.text: Japan sent some four hundred air conditioners or something as relief. Which makes absolutely no sense, right?

quiz.a: The fruit of the poisonous tree doctrine, which Shah believes dates from 1938.
